questions.question: What is the codomain of a function?
options: The set of inputs of the function.
The set where all outputs must lie.
Only the outputs actually attained by the function.
A rule for differentiating the function.

questions.question: How is the range of a function related to its codomain?
options: The range is always a subset of the codomain.
The codomain is always a subset of the range.
The range and codomain are always disjoint.
The range is the same as the domain.

questions.question: For $f(x) = x^2$ defined as $f\colon \mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$, what is the codomain?
The same formula $f(x) = x^2$ is given with codomain $[0,+\infty)$. What is the codomain?
Why does the codomain matter for surjectivity?
options: Surjectivity depends only on the formula, whatever codomain is chosen.
Surjectivity depends on whether each codomain value is hit only once.
Surjectivity depends on whether the range fills the chosen codomain.
Surjectivity depends on whether the domain fills the chosen codomain.

questions.question: Can changing only the codomain of a function produce a different function?
options: Changing the codomain never affects the function.
Changing the codomain can define a different function.
Changing the codomain changes the formula but not the target set.
Changing the codomain makes the domain empty.

questions.question: For $f\colon \mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ with $f(x) = x^2$, which set must contain the range?
Which notation explicitly gives $Y$ as the codomain?
Which distinction is important for the codomain concept?
options: Codomain is the set of attained outputs; range is the declared target.
Codomain is the set of inputs; range is the set of actual outputs.
The range may contain outputs that lie outside the codomain.
Codomain is chosen with the function; range is the actual outputs.

questions.question: Why is the formula $f(x) = x^2$ alone not enough to fully specify the function?
options: The range must be stated separately from the formula.
Domain and codomain are also part of the function.
Only the domain is missing; the codomain is always $\mathbb{R}$.
The formula forces the codomain to be $[0,\infty)$.

questions.question: For the formula $f(x)=x^2$, which choice of codomain defines a function different from $f\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$?
Suppose a function has codomain $Y$ and range $R_f$. Which relation is always true?
Which property of a function is equivalent to its range equalling its codomain?
For $f\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ with $f(x)=x^2$, how do range and codomain compare?
options: The codomain is smaller than the range

questions.question: Why can changing the codomain matter?
Which property is guaranteed if a function's codomain is replaced by its range?
For $f\colon\mathbb{R}\to[0,+\infty)$, $f(x)=x^2$, what is the codomain?
Is the codomain determined by the formula $f(x)$ alone?
options: No; it is determined by the domain

questions.question: Why can the same formula with a different codomain define a different function?
options: Because a different codomain changes the range of the function
Because changing the codomain changes every input
Because a function includes its domain, codomain, and rule
Because functions are equal only when their ranges are equal

questions.question: For $f\colon\mathbb{R}\to[0,+\infty)$ with $f(x)=x^2$, which statement about surjectivity is correct?
options: It is not surjective because negative numbers are missing from the codomain.
